title: Team Members Who Turn Off Their Cameras During Virtual Calls
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the now-common practice of joining virtual meetings with cameras off, and argues leaders should push back against treating it as a neutral individual choice. While it acknowledges legitimate exceptions — poor connectivity, driving, an inconvenient time zone — it argues that camera-off participation reliably correlates with fewer comments, lower engagement, and team members being effectively overlooked in discussion. The piece contends that visual cues are important enough to communication and interpretation that defaulting to "camera optional" quietly erodes team cohesion, and recommends leaders set an explicit expectation that cameras stay on absent a good reason not to.
points: Camera-off participation is linked to measurably lower engagement: fewer comments, less visibility, and team members becoming an afterthought in discussion.
The article names legitimate exceptions (connectivity, driving, time zone) but argues these shouldn't become the unexamined default for everyone.
The recommended policy shift is from "camera optional" to "camera on unless there's a good reason not to" — reframing the default itself.
Face-to-face interaction, even mediated through video, is argued to foster stronger connection and engagement than voice-only participation.
quotes: The dependence on video or virtual calls to conduct team meetings isn’t going away.
Leaders are often disappointed in this choice but accept it as a workable way to get everyone to join the call.
Team members who are off video make fewer comments, are generally less engaged, and are often overlooked during the discussion.
A better rule for most teams and leaders is to ask people to engage fully and turn the camera on unless there is a very good reason not to.
Good leaders understand the impact facial cues and gestures, even on video, have on the meanings people ascribe to one another.
Individual preferences should never be held in higher regard than what the team needs to be the most effective.
